facts.text: Humpback whales often jump above the waves and hit the water with their long fins or tails.
Some humpback populations travel about 5,000 miles between warm tropical waters, where they mate and give birth, and cold feeding grounds.
Humpbacks feed on krill and small fish.
The black-and-white pattern on the underside of each humpback's tail is unique, so scientists use it to identify individual whales.
Industrial whaling in the 20th century killed many kinds of whales, including blue, fin, sperm, minke and humpback whales.
Before commercial whaling was stopped, nearly every humpback population had shrunk sharply; most had lost over 95 percent of their numbers.
About 25,000 humpbacks were caught in the western South Atlantic, off Brazil, over about 12 years in the early 1900s.
The western South Atlantic humpback population fell to about 450 whales by the 1950s.
Humpbacks gained protection in the 1960s after scientists saw their numbers dropping around the world.
A moratorium (pause) on all commercial whaling, set by the International Whaling Commission, began in the mid-1980s; it gave further protection and played a major role in humpback recovery.

An International Whaling Commission assessment carried out between 2006 and 2015 had estimated that the western South Atlantic population had recovered to only about 30 percent of its size before hunting.
A 2019 study using new data on past catches, genetics and life history estimated the population at about 25,000 whales, about 93 percent of its size before hunting.
Of the 14 humpback populations (distinct population segments) recognized under U.S. law, nine are no longer listed as endangered or threatened; four are endangered and one is threatened.
Humpbacks today face threats from getting caught in fishing gear, being hit by ships, and underwater noise.
Whales compete with penguins and seals for krill, so the recovery of humpbacks may affect other animals.

Derived from the dataset: the most whales were killed in the 1960s (703,235); more were killed in the 2000s (18,141) than in the 1990s (10,300); more in the 1950s (613,862) than in the 1930s (403,287).
